In case you haven't noticed, there has been a lot of members of Congress traveling to Taiwan recently. And some of those trips have been causing quite a stir. If you think back to last August when then Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi went to Taiwan, it was a huge bruja. And it escalated with a lot of threats coming from the Chinese Communist Party, directed at Speaker Pelosi's plane. And after Speaker Pelosi's delegation left Taiwan, you saw the People's Liberation Army, China's military, step up a lot of exercises inside of Taiwan's internal waters. And that was probably the most belligerent of a whole suite of retaliatory options that Beijing levied against Taipei to punish them for accepting Speaker Pelosi. So this caused a big rift in the D.C. China community of, was it the right decision for Speaker Pelosi to go? Was it wise? Was it not wise? Putting the timing of the trip aside, I was and still am of the farm opinion that as soon as her trip leaked and became public, she had no choice but to go. Members of Congress have been traveling and visiting Taiwan for a long time, and under no circumstances should we allow Beijing to set the terms of who visits Taiwan, when they visit Taiwan. That is a decision for American officials only in concert with their counterparts in Taiwan. So after Pelosi's trip, there was this huge focus on Taiwan and congressional visits there. And there were a number of members of Congress who traveled last year and even more have visited this year. And I'm really excited to share a conversation that I had with a member who just returned from the Indo-Pacific and from Taiwan, Senator Todd Young from Indiana. He has a long track record of being a leader in the Senate on China policy. For those of you who've been following some of the inside the beltway legislating on China policy recently, You will definitely know that he was like the guy along with Senator Schumer, who is the majority leader in the Senate. Senator Young was the guy on semiconductor legislation that passed Congress. It's called the Chips and Science Act. We talk about the chips bill at the end of our conversation. So if you stick around to the very end, the senator will talk about the procedure of how that think whole mammoth legislation got done and he'll talk about implementation. But the top of the interview is all about Taiwan. Things are definitely heating up and are heating up. So I'm grateful that the senator was willing to share his perspective. And not just about Taiwan, he also visited Japan right after his time in Taiwan. and we get into that as well. And I think what you have waiting for you here is a really illustrative conversation, less about the politics surrounding US-China relations and more about the policy issues that our friends and allies are very worried about and conscious of every single day. And Senator Young has a lot of solutions in mind that he's legislated on. So anyways, with all that preface, I think it was a really wonderful conversation and I'm glad to share it with each of you. So let's get into it. Senator Young, it is a true pleasure to be speaking with you today. Thanks for coming on the podcast. It's great to be with you, Michael. Thank you. My pleasure. Okay. So let's jump in here. You just came back from Taiwan, which has seen a flurry of congressional activity and congressional visits recently. When you came back, you said that you think every member of Congress should make it out there, that everyone should take the opportunity to go visit Taiwan. And something else you said that certainly caught my attention and I think the attention of many, in a conversation with some folks at Politico, you said that you're increasingly convinced that the next five years are really important for Taiwan's security. And you said that in the context of China's ambitions towards Taiwan. So I'm curious to ask you, at the very top, what is convincing you that the next five years are so crucial and so important for the future of Taiwan?
